To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

stress activates the brain stem noradrenergic system, which can activate the hypothalami parvocellular neurons that secrete corticotropin‐ releasing factor (CRF), and that the CRF can, in turn, activate the noradrenergie system, which can further activate the parvocellular CRF neurons in a feed‐forward fashion.

stress activates both CRF neurons in PVN and LC‐NE neurons; the CRF neurons in brain areas such as PVN and amygdala project to the area containing LC‐NE neurons and that CRF activates the LC‐neurons; the LC‐NE neurons, in turn, stimulate the CRF neurons.
CRF and NE are activated during stress and interact reciprocally.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neurochemical and neuroanatomic basis of the interactions between CRF and NE in the brain.
the role of CRF in the regulation of NE neurons in the LC and other brain areas.
the brain circuits involved in CRF‐NE interactions during stress and with the possible role of these interactions in stress‐related behavioral responses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CRF‐NE interactions during stress are complex and that further studies are necessary.
the CRF‐NE interactions are complex and are not fully understood.
the brain circuits involved in CRF‐NE interactions during stress are complex and that the interactions are not yet fully understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
stress activates both CRF and NE neurons, but the interactions between the two systems may not always be the same.
the brain circuits that are activated during acute stress are not sensitized by repeated stress.
CRF and NE interact in the brain during stress, and the interaction may be bidirectional.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain circuitry involved in CRF‐NE interactions during stress is complex.
CRF‐NE interactions are complex, and the effects are not necessarily the same in every situation.
the stress‐activated CRF‐NE system may be a promising target for the development of novel antidepressant drugs.
